articles.title: A digital publication sheds light on Turkey’s prison system
articles.summary: “For the relatives of people in prison, as well as for national and international human rights organizations and agencies, the information provided by the Prison Agenda publication can be vital.”
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In Turkey, a team of two journalists and human rights activists launched a digital publication, Prison Agenda, to report on what is happening inside the country’s prisons and prison system, information that is often hidden from the Turkish public and the world.

As the Nordic Monitor noted in 2025, Turkey’s prison population has reached an unprecedented level. Citing figures from the Directorate General of Prisons and Houses of Detention, the website states that as of September 1, 2025, Turkish prisons hold 419,194 individuals. This includes 356,710 convicted prisoners and 62,484 people in pretrial detention. The figure exceeds the official capacity of 295,000 and places immense strain on the country’s penal system.

Le Monde also wrote in 2026 that a commissioned report on prison conditions among Council of Europe member states showed that France and Turkey each had 131 inmates for every 100 places, making them the two most overcrowded prison systems.

For the relatives of people in prison, as well as for national and international human rights organizations and agencies, the information provided by the Prison Agenda publication can be vital. A similar organization — Russia Behind Bars — used to work in Russia. While it did not function exclusively as a publication, it received letters from prisoners and their relatives, published news about torture or other human rights violations, and reported how the prison population had been drafted, in the hundreds of thousands, to fight Russia’s war with Ukraine. Unfortunately, it had to shut down its work within Russia because of the regime’s prosecution, but it continues to inform from abroad.

Civil society organizations, such as the publication about Prisons and Prisoners, are vital to the country and the world; they need to continue their important work within one of the most opaque systems in the world.

Global Voices interviewed one of Prison Agenda’s founder, Ahmet Kavruk, by email.

GV: Please tell us about your organization, and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Ahmet Kavruk (AK): Prison Agenda is a digital publication that covers data on Turkey’s prisons, legislative changes relating to prisons, and human rights violations within them. It is guided by an independent, rights-focused approach to journalism.

We launched in January 2026. Our aim is to make the often complicated and scattered information about prisons more accessible to the public by presenting it in a clear and understandable way, and to highlight the human stories behind the statistics.

Shortly after launching in January, we reached a crossroads. We could either continue as a passion project, publishing solely in Turkish, which would be easier to sustain, but would not fulfil our potential, or evolve into a publishing model that would require more intensive work, but enable us to reach a wider audience.

It was precisely at this decision-making stage that we came across the Digital Spark call for proposals. It was one of the few support programmes capable of creating space for initiatives working in specific and often overlooked fields, such as prisons. We, therefore, drew up a plan and, should we be accepted into Digital Sparks, began to focus on the question, ‘How can we grow the Prison Agenda?’

We were particularly impressed by Digital Spark’s approach, which focuses on amplifying the voices of marginalized groups and strengthening civic participation. The fact that the project’s core objectives aligned so closely with our own area of work was a decisive factor in our decision to join the programme.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

AK: We are currently a team of two. We are both individuals with over 10 years’ experience working and producing within the prison sector in various capacities. We were aware of the growing problems in Turkey’s prisons. Through our voluntary work, professional lives and social networks, we have been trying to raise awareness of these issues.

However, our work in this field revealed not only these problems, but also a significant shortcoming. No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicated this information to the public using data. The data was scattered, technical and often difficult to access. Meanwhile, media interest tended to intensify only when there was new legislation or a high-profile incident.

Drawing on our background in journalism and our experience in human rights monitoring, we believed we could address this gap. We, therefore, launched Prison Agenda, aiming to present existing information to the public in a clear, accessible, rights-focused manner.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

AK: The most significant change for us during this project was launching our bilingual publications. By switching to English, we were able to reach beyond our existing Turkish audience and connect with a very different group of readers. The feedback from this new audience further strengthened our belief in the project’s potential.

While we initially had just one e-newsletter, we diversified our publications over time, increasing our regular e-newsletters to three. Today, Prison Agenda has evolved from a publication that shares news into a comprehensive digital media organisation that produces investigative reports, data analyses, data visualisations, thematic content, and opinion pieces.

This transformation aligns with our initial project goals of bilingual publishing and data-driven content production. In the first six months, our Turkish and English newsletters reached a total of 435 subscribers.

AK: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

AK: While our Turkish-language publications are mainly followed by the press, legislators and civil society, we have noticed that our English-language publications are attracting the attention of diplomatic missions from various countries and international-level bureaucrats. This was a significant development for us as it created an opportunity to raise awareness of prison issues in Turkey within a wider international network.

Throughout the project, we received collaboration proposals from different organisations and groups. The number of news articles citing our data and content increased, raising Prison Agenda's profile. Additionally, we started providing advice on data, sources and content to journalists reporting on prisons.

This has ensured that the information we produce is not limited to our own readers, but is made available within a wider ecosystem. We hope the network of readers and stakeholders established by Prison Agenda will help to raise awareness of prisoners’ rights and the need for humane prison conditions. The project’s aim was, indeed, to strengthen civil oversight and accountability by making information more accessible.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

AK: Prisons are, by their very nature, a rather closed field of work, with limited overlap with many other areas of rights. For this reason, we are not always able to collaborate with other civil society organisations.

One of the most significant opportunities that Digital Sparks has created for us is the chance to share a space with different civil society organisations and learn about their work first-hand. We have met groups working on issues outside our own field, developing different methods, and those who are just starting out. These encounters have enabled us to share knowledge and view our own work from an outside perspective.

One of the most significant realisations for us during this process was that civil society is much larger and broader than we had previously realised. Because Prison Agenda works in a very specific field, we realised that we were sometimes limited to our immediate circle. However, Digital Sparks showed us that this field is much broader and that there are far more areas where different struggles can intersect.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

AK: Digital Spark was the first support we received. Although we had previously been involved in various projects as part of a team, this was the first time we had been part of a project where the full responsibility rested directly with us. For this reason, it was also a new learning experience for us.

This was actually the part that challenged us the most. We learnt that a project is not limited to simply producing content and activities; it also requires managing its budget, administrative processes, reporting and responsibilities.

One of the most tangible things we learnt during this process was financial reporting. While our previous experience in this area was limited, carrying out the reporting processes required by the project provided us with valuable practical experience.

Consequently, Digital Sparks was not merely a project through which we developed Prison Agenda’s publishing capacity; it was also a significant experience in a small team transforming into a structure capable of standing on its own two feet, managing its responsibilities, and planning for the future.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

AK: Although we’re a very new organisation, we’re just as eager and enthusiastic. We have many options before us that could take us in different directions, as well as ideas that we’re keen to develop.

For example, we’re currently refining a public prison database project, and we’re also preparing to run a training course on prison journalism in the new year. We have a wide variety of datasets at our disposal that we want to make accessible to a wider audience. In the long term, we also plan to increase the number of areas we cover and deepen the content we produce in these fields.

We believe that we have not yet reached our natural limits. The digital capacity we have developed through Digital Sparks has opened up significant scope for us to expand these limits. In the near future, we intend to use the knowledge and experience we have gained to prioritise our readers, understand their requirements, and integrate their feedback into our editorial strategy.

Our aim is to transform the Prison Agenda into a structure that produces more content and enables more people to access information on prisons, bringing together different stakeholders in the process.
articles.reasoning: The article describes the launch and growth of Prison Agenda, a digital publication that provides vital, independent, and accessible information on Turkey's overcrowded and opaque prison system. This initiative enhances transparency, raises awareness about human rights violations, and strengthens civil society oversight in a significant and challenging context. The publication's bilingual approach and data-driven content have expanded its reach to international audiences, increasing its impact and potential for advocacy. The story focuses on a concrete, meaningful effort with broad societal relevance and sufficient detail.
articles.personality_title: New digital publication reveals hidden truths about Turkey’s overcrowded prisons
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Turkey’s prisons are severely overcrowded, holding over 419,000 people despite having space for only 295,000. Information about conditions inside these prisons is often hard to find or understand, leaving families, human rights groups, and the public in the dark.

**What happened** – In January 2026, two journalists and human rights activists launched Prison Agenda, a digital publication that collects, explains, and shares data about Turkey’s prisons. Supported by the Digital Spark program, they expanded their work from Turkish-only to bilingual content in Turkish and English. This helped Prison Agenda reach not just local readers but also international diplomats and human rights organizations.

**Impact** – Prison Agenda fills a rare gap by providing clear, independent updates on prison conditions and human rights issues. Their work helps families of prisoners and civil society groups stay informed. By sharing data and investigative reports, they encourage public awareness and civil oversight in a system known for secrecy and overcrowding.

**What's next step** – The team plans to develop a public database of prison information and launch training on prison journalism. They want to create more detailed content and grow their audience, using feedback to improve their work. Their goal is to become a stronger, independent source of information connecting different groups concerned with prison conditions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Prison Agenda is a new digital platform making Turkey’s overcrowded prison system more transparent and accessible to both national and international communities.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle publication numérique révèle la réalité cachée des prisons surpeuplées de Turquie
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les prisons turques sont gravement surpeuplées, accueillant plus de 419 000 personnes alors qu'elles ne disposent que de 295 000 places. Les informations sur les conditions à l'intérieur sont souvent difficiles à trouver ou à comprendre, laissant les familles, les groupes de défense des droits humains et le public dans l'ignorance.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – En janvier 2026, deux journalistes et militants des droits humains ont lancé Prison Agenda, une publication numérique qui collecte, explique et partage des données sur les prisons turques. Soutenue par le programme Digital Spark, leur publication est passée du turc à un contenu bilingue turc-anglais, ce qui leur a permis de toucher non seulement un public local, mais aussi des diplomates et organisations internationales.

**Impact** – Prison Agenda comble un vide en fournissant des informations claires et indépendantes sur les conditions carcérales et les violations des droits humains. Leur travail aide les familles de détenus et les organisations de la société civile à rester informées. En partageant des données et des enquêtes, ils encouragent la sensibilisation publique et la surveillance civile dans un système connu pour son opacité et sa surpopulation.

**Prochaine étape** – L'équipe prévoit de développer une base de données publique sur les prisons et de lancer une formation au journalisme carcéral. Ils souhaitent créer un contenu plus détaillé et élargir leur audience, en utilisant les retours pour améliorer leur travail. Leur objectif est de devenir une source d'information indépendante plus forte, reliant différents acteurs concernés par les conditions en prison.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Prison Agenda est une nouvelle plateforme numérique qui rend le système carcéral surpeuplé de Turquie plus transparent et accessible aux communautés nationales et internationales.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva publicación digital revela verdades ocultas sobre las prisiones sobrepobladas de Turquía
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las prisiones de Turquía están gravemente sobrepobladas, con más de 419,000 personas alojadas cuando solo hay espacio para 295,000. La información sobre las condiciones dentro de estas prisiones es difícil de encontrar o entender, dejando a familias, grupos de derechos humanos y al público sin saber qué ocurre.

**Qué pasó** – En enero de 2026, dos periodistas y activistas de derechos humanos lanzaron Prison Agenda, una publicación digital que recopila, explica y comparte datos sobre las prisiones turcas. Con el apoyo del programa Digital Spark, ampliaron su contenido de solo turco a bilingüe en turco e inglés, alcanzando no solo a lectores locales sino también a diplomáticos y organizaciones internacionales.

**Impacto** – Prison Agenda llena un vacío al ofrecer información clara e independiente sobre las condiciones carcelarias y violaciones de derechos humanos. Su trabajo ayuda a las familias de los presos y a las organizaciones civiles a mantenerse informadas. Al compartir datos y reportajes de investigación, fomentan la conciencia pública y la supervisión civil en un sistema conocido por su opacidad y sobrepoblación.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo planea desarrollar una base de datos pública sobre prisiones y lanzar un curso de periodismo penitenciario. Quieren crear contenido más detallado y aumentar su audiencia, usando las opiniones para mejorar su trabajo. Su meta es convertirse en una fuente independiente y fuerte que conecte a diferentes grupos preocupados por las condiciones carcelarias.

**Resumen en una frase** – Prison Agenda es una nueva plataforma digital que hace que el sistema penitenciario sobrepoblado de Turquía sea más transparente y accesible para las comunidades nacionales e internacionales.

articles.title: Foreign defence contractors will need to invest in UK under new rules
articles.summary: Foreign firms awarded large defence contracts will need to invest an equal value back into the UK, Wes Streeting announces.
articles.content:
Foreign firms awarded large defence contracts will need to invest an equal value back into the UK to create "bang for the British buck", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has announced.

Under the new rules, companies receiving more than £50m will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.

It comes as the government continues to face pressure to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, an objective some opposition MPs and defence analysts have questioned its ability to deliver.

Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules would help achieve this target given it "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".

"What we're aiming to do is on the most valuable of those contracts worth £50m or more, is to try and get benefit for Britain, bang for the British buck back here at home," he added.

The investment stipulations for foreign businesses, which the government described as its "offset strategy", are hoped to increase investment in Britain's defence industry.

The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said in a statement.

Countries, including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands, have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the statement continued.

It added: "The government is prioritising buying British defence contracts wherever possible.

"Where it must buy defence equipment from overseas, this new approach will ensure British workers and businesses still benefit."

Streeting and Chancellor John Healey will unveil the new rules on a visit to the UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow.

The policy appears designed to make the proposed extra investment in defence more politically palatable, rather than committing to outright increased direct cuts and spending.
articles.reasoning: The new UK government policy requiring foreign defence contractors to reinvest an equal value into British factories, jobs, and training represents a significant positive economic and social impact. It promotes domestic job creation, skills development, and economic growth, benefiting a broad public beyond a niche group. The policy is clearly described with details on thresholds, implementation timeline, and international precedents, showing substantive context and meaningful scope.
articles.personality_title: UK requires foreign defence firms to invest locally under new rules
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The UK government wants to spend more on defence and support its own economy. To do this, it aims to make sure foreign companies that win big defence contracts also help British businesses and workers.

**What happened** – Defence Secretary Wes Streeting announced that foreign firms awarded defence contracts worth more than £50 million must invest the same amount back into the UK. This investment will support British factories, create jobs, and provide training. The new rules will start being applied from April 2027 and will be decided case by case.

**Impact** – This policy helps the UK get more value from its defence spending. Instead of money leaving the country, it stays and helps grow the British defence industry. It also creates new jobs and skills for British workers. Other countries like Poland and Norway use similar rules, showing this is a trusted approach.

**What's next step** – The government will start applying these rules in 2027 and continue to focus on buying British defence products when possible. Officials, including the Defence Secretary and Chancellor, will promote the new policy during visits to UK defence factories.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UK will now require foreign defence contractors to invest equally in Britain, boosting jobs and industry while supporting national defence spending goals.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le Royaume-Uni exige des investissements locaux des entreprises de défense étrangères
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le gouvernement britannique souhaite augmenter ses dépenses de défense tout en soutenant son économie locale. Pour cela, il veut que les entreprises étrangères qui remportent de gros contrats de défense aident aussi les entreprises et les travailleurs britanniques.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le secrétaire à la Défense, Wes Streeting, a annoncé que les entreprises étrangères obtenant des contrats de défense de plus de 50 millions de livres devront investir un montant équivalent au Royaume-Uni. Cet investissement soutiendra les usines britanniques, créera des emplois et offrira des formations. Ces nouvelles règles seront appliquées à partir d'avril 2027, au cas par cas.

**Impact** – Cette politique permet au Royaume-Uni de mieux profiter de ses dépenses de défense. Au lieu que l'argent parte à l'étranger, il reste dans le pays pour développer l'industrie de défense britannique. Cela crée aussi de nouveaux emplois et compétences pour les travailleurs locaux. Des pays comme la Pologne et la Norvège utilisent déjà des règles similaires, ce qui montre que cette approche est fiable.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement commencera à appliquer ces règles en 2027 et continuera de privilégier l'achat de produits de défense britanniques quand c'est possible. Les responsables, dont le secrétaire à la Défense et le chancelier, présenteront cette nouvelle politique lors de visites dans des usines britanniques.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le Royaume-Uni demandera désormais aux entreprises étrangères de défense d'investir autant dans le pays, ce qui favorisera l'emploi et l'industrie tout en soutenant les objectifs de dépenses nationales en défense.
articles.personality_title_es: Reino Unido exige inversión local a empresas extranjeras de defensa bajo nuevas reglas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El gobierno del Reino Unido quiere gastar más en defensa y apoyar su propia economía. Para lograrlo, busca que las empresas extranjeras que ganen grandes contratos de defensa también ayuden a las empresas y trabajadores británicos.

**Qué pasó** – El secretario de Defensa, Wes Streeting, anunció que las empresas extranjeras que reciban contratos de defensa por más de 50 millones de libras deberán invertir un monto igual en el Reino Unido. Esta inversión apoyará fábricas británicas, creará empleos y ofrecerá capacitación. Las nuevas reglas se aplicarán desde abril de 2027 y se decidirán caso por caso.

**Impacto** – Esta política ayuda al Reino Unido a obtener más valor de su gasto en defensa. En lugar de que el dinero salga del país, se queda y ayuda a crecer la industria de defensa británica. También crea nuevos empleos y habilidades para los trabajadores británicos. Otros países como Polonia y Noruega usan reglas similares, mostrando que es un método probado.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno empezará a aplicar estas reglas en 2027 y seguirá enfocándose en comprar productos de defensa británicos cuando sea posible. Funcionarios, incluyendo al Secretario de Defensa y al Canciller, promoverán la nueva política durante visitas a fábricas de defensa en el Reino Unido.

**Resumen en una frase** – El Reino Unido requerirá que los contratistas extranjeros de defensa inviertan igual en el país, impulsando empleos e industria mientras apoyan las metas nacionales de gasto en defensa.
